newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cuba attacks U.S. island states fear submersion.
newsitem.headline: Cuba attacks U.S. island states fear submersion.

text.p: Small island states told the U.N. Earth Summit on Tuesday they could be washed away unless action is taken against global warming while Cuba blamed U.S. "capitalist greed" for global ecological damage.

The speaker of Cuba's parliament, Ricardo Alarcon, in a fierce attack on Washington and rich states in general, said, "capitalist greed is the principal cause of the unjust world and of the severe damage to nature which is threatening the survival of humankind today."

He also sounded a familiar Third World theme at the 173-nation conference when he attacked rich countries for not giving enough funds to the Third World to ensure development without environmental damage.

"For those who accumulated their wealth through the exploitation of the Third World it is not a matter of assisting but of returning part of what they plundered," said Alarcon, a former foreign minister.

The week-long, 173-nation conference, to be addressed by more than 60 prime ministers and presidents, is taking stock of what has been done to prevent ecological disaster since the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.
Several small island states sounded alarm bells about the slow pace towards reducing greenhouse gases.
These nations, including Cyprus, Caribbean nations and Pacific archipelagos, say their survival is threatened by the rise of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases.

President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom of the Indian Ocean Maldives told the summit that "80 per cent of the low-lying islands such as those of the Maldives and many in the Pacific Ocean would be totally submerged," if global warming was not curbed.
"The process may be too gradual to make sensational headlines, but the threat, nevertheless, would be no less real," he said.
Scientists predict sea levels will rise between 30 centimetres (12 inches) and 100 centimetres (40 inches) by 2,100 as the planet grows warmer, if greenhouse gases are not reduced.
Global warming causes melting of the polar ice caps, which raises ocean levels, intensifies storms and kills coral reefs.
On Monday, President Jacob Nena of the Pacific Micronesia chain said rising sea levels and more frequent storms had wiped out food sources and some smaller atolls had already had to be abandoned.
"Help us, help all of us, including yourselves, to see that the legacy of Rio is not lost," he said.

Governments are negotiating a new treaty to cut back greenhouse gases. The Europeans have set specific goals but neither the United States, Canada nor Japan have agreed to their target of reducing emissions by 15 percent below the 1990 levels by 2,010.
The small island states want this raised to 20 percent.

President Bill Clinton will set 50-year goals for reducing global warming when he addresses the summit on Thursday, rather than agreeing to short term targets, according to Under Secretary of State Tim Wirth.

Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien told the conference his country would "not meet the year 2,000 targets for stabilising greenhouse gas emissions" because the structure "of our economy poses particular challenges in this regard."
